item.title: CPU Pipeline Stalls: Diagnosing and Mitigating Self-Modifying Code (SMC) Penalties
item.description:
“CPU Pipeline Stalls: Diagnosing and Mitigating Self-Modifying Code (SMC) Penalties”

How can one pinpoint performance loss attributed to SMC on modern Intel processors, and what architectural details govern this penalty?

Deep Dive into SMC Detection and Performance Impact

The accepted approach for identifying this issue involves monitoring specific performance counters exposed by the CPU.

Primary Diagnostic Metric: You should check the MACHINE_CLEARS.SMC performance counter. This counter is part of the broader MACHINE_CLEARS event, which logs instances where the processor pipeline must be entirely flushed and restarted following the last retired instruction.

item.title: x86-64 Addressing Limits: Virtual vs. Physical Space via PAE
item.description:
“x86-64 Addressing Limits: Virtual vs. Physical Space via PAE”

When operating systems run in 64-bit mode on modern CPUs, the mechanism used to translate virtual addresses to physical addresses is heavily influenced by the Physical Address Extension (PAE). This feature, initially designed to expand the addressable memory space beyond the 4GB barrier for 32-bit systems, introduces a multi-level table structure essential for handling the vast 64-bit address space. Why, then, are we currently restricted in our visible virtual address space?

item.title: CPU Partial Register Renaming: Haswell vs. Skylake and Beyond
item.description:
“CPU Partial Register Renaming: Haswell vs. Skylake and Beyond”

How do modern CPUs, specifically Intel’s Haswell and Skylake architectures, handle operations on partial registers (like AL, AH) and how does this differ from earlier designs such as Sandy Bridge and Ivy Bridge? What are the implications for performance, and what are the practical ways to leverage or avoid these behaviors in assembly code?

The core of the issue lies in how CPUs manage register renaming for partial register accesses. Unlike older designs where lower byte registers (e.g., AL) might be renamed independently of their wider counterparts (e.g., RAX), newer architectures like Haswell and Skylake often merge these operations.

item.title: MOV Elimination: Does it Really Have Zero Latency on Modern CPUs?
item.description:
“MOV Elimination: Does it Really Have Zero Latency on Modern CPUs?”

Does the MOV instruction truly offer zero latency on modern CPUs, or is it a nuanced behavior influenced by microarchitecture and specific instruction patterns? This exploration delves into the mechanics and observed performance impacts of MOV elimination, supported by practical assembly examples and benchmarking.

The core concept of MOV elimination, often referred to as register renaming for MOV, allows certain copy operations to bypass actual execution units. Instead, the operation is handled during the instruction issue or rename stage. This effectively removes the latency and execution port usage associated with a typical instruction.

item.title: Intel Micro-Fusion: Addressing Modes & Performance Impact
item.description:
“Intel Micro-Fusion: Addressing Modes & Performance Impact”

Delving into the intricate world of CPU microarchitectures, particularly Intel’s processors, reveals fascinating behaviors related to micro-fusion. This process involves combining multiple instructions into a single micro-operation (uop) to enhance execution efficiency. A key factor influencing this behavior is the addressing mode used by instructions. How do different addressing modes impact micro-fusion, and what are the observed performance implications across various Intel microarchitectures like Sandybridge, Haswell, and Skylake?
